defects: No strip files were supplied, so in-shot motion was judged only from frames.jpg and pairs.jpg. Most credit cards look like static holds that are cut away on the beat.
In the 'WRITTEN & DIRECTED BY' pair, the two frames 1/6 s apart are identical: a dead hold with no in-shot motion.
The title-card pair also barely moves. The only changes are a chromatic flicker and the 'A FILM BY' line popping in, with no eased build.
The ending breaks the title apart by deleting letters ('NIG CH US'). Letters vanish rather than move off with follow-through, and the last frame reads as an unfinished state.
The 6-8.5 s riser is flat broadband white noise with no tonal shape. It cuts off abruptly at about 8.6 s, which reads as a stock build-and-drop.
The RGB-split fringing on 'ISAK LINDQVIST' and on the title letters softens edges and costs legibility. It is applied as a filter, not built into the design.
The dot-matrix and LED-grid letterforms (the H in CHORUS, the dotted HT and US) risk moiré and shimmer when compressed. The blue grid cells at the crop are already uneven.

Each card uses a different type family and palette (condensed pattern, RGB-split grotesk, gilt Didone italic, blackletter on paper, LED grid). That variety is deliberate, but no single frame is restrained.
gaps: Motion is cut-driven, not choreographed. Each name is a static style card swapped on the beat, with no transitions built into the material, no eased entrances, overlap or follow-through, and nothing travelling from a credit card into its letter in the title. The payoff idea (each credit's treatment becomes one letter of NIGHT CHORUS) is told by cuts instead of shown through movement.

The sound is a click track of transients plus a generic noise riser and drop. There is little arrangement development, and the sound design doesn't match each card's material (gilt, paper, LED, op-art). It syncs to the cuts but has no musical voice or dynamic shaping beyond one swell.

The structure has a flat 0.47 s cadence, then a 4.2 s title hold that ends by letters simply disappearing. A top studio would vary the rhythm across the credits, land the title with weight (settle and overshoot), and end on a clean, composed lockup that rhymes with the op-art opening rather than a half-erased frame.
